newsitem.title: DUBAI: India's Dunlop chief says no management discord.
newsitem.headline: India's Dunlop chief says no management discord.

text.p: Dunlop India Ltd chairman Manohar Chhabria denied on Thursday that management discord had triggered the resignation of the tyre-maker's managing director Murli Shukla earlier this week.
"There is no personal disagreement between me and Dr M.D. Shukla," Chhabria told Reuters at his Dubai base.
Shukla's resignation on Monday followed a week of open confrontation between Shukla at the company's Calcutta, India headquarters and the Dubai-based Chhabria.
Shukla, contacted by telephone at his home in Calcutta, refused to answer any questions.
Chhabria said that following Shukla's resignation, chief financial officer Anju Madeka had resigned on Tuesday. "She was asked to give certain information which was not forthcoming."
Madeka told Reuters by telephone from Calcutta: "All information that was required was given."
The company's Monday statement said an audit of management and financial performance had been ordered after Shukla's exit.
"The board has also decided with a view to bringing in further transparency in Dunlop to have an audit done of Dunlop's management and financial performance," the statement said.
Chhabria said the audit was a "precautionary move".
"We don't anticipate any foul play. No manipulation, no surprises are expected. As a prudent policy we have decided to do this to increase transparency because of press speculation."
Former CFO Madeka said: "There has been no financial impropriety."

The row erupted when Shukla was quoted in Indian newspapers as saying Chhabria had summoned three other top executives of the blue-chip company to Dubai and insulted them. Chhabria controls 44 percent of Dunlop India.
The denouement came on Monday. A terse Dunlop announcement said Shukla had resigned and the company had appointed a panel of three directors as an interim measure.
The committee will initiate steps to strengthen the management team and the executive board, it added.
Chhabria said Indian newspaper reports about Shukla's "revolt" were speculative.
"The press has been speculating and has been hostile to him and the company. Dr Shukla honourably apologised for misunderstandings via the media," Chhabria said.
He said the three-man committee would ensure there was no disruption in the company's affairs and nominate a replacement for Shukla.

Chhabria said business was running normally and he expected the company to make net profits of between 450 million and 500 million rupees in fiscal 1996/97 ending March 31, up from 390 million in the 15 months to March 31 1996.
"It should be in the range of 450-500 million rupees for 1996/97," he said.
Chhabria told Reuters in October that he was looking for finance for two, new projects worth $250 million to produce tyres and refrigeration equipment in the United Arab Emirates.
He said then that his Jumbo International Holding Ltd would start negotiations with financial institutions as soon as detailed studies were completed.

Chhabria set up Jumbo International some 20 years ago in Dubai. With net assets at $700 million, the group now has wide interests including the manufacture and distribution of consumer goods and machinery, travel, shipping and real-estate.

It is registered in Bermuda but the business is run from Dubai. Seven subsidiaries, fully or partly owned by Jumbo, have an annual turnover of $1.5 billion and cover Bahrain, the UAE, Oman, Britain, Germany, Japan, India, South Korea, and the United States.
